summary: Describes a framework for Realm Specific IP (RSIP), an alternative to network address translation. With RSIP, a host borrows addressing parameters from a gateway so packets keep their end-to-end integrity. The document covers implementation issues, deployment scenarios, and interaction with other layer-three protocols. It is an experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: Instead of a receptionist swapping your name tag on every letter, you borrow a real name tag from the front desk, so your letters arrive unchanged.

questions: alternative to nat that preserves end-to-end
subtitle: Let a private host borrow real addresses and ports from a gateway instead of having a NAT rewrite its packets.

tldr.problem: NAT rewrites packet headers, which breaks end-to-end integrity and needs an application layer gateway (ALG) for each application that embeds addresses in its payload.
tldr.mechanism: With Realm Specific IP (RSIP), a host leases addresses, and optionally ports, from an RSIP gateway and tunnels its packets to the gateway, which strips the outer header and sends the inner packet on.
tldr.outcome: RSIP is described as a fix of sorts to NAT, not a long-term answer to address shortage, and it brings complications. The memo is Experimental.

today: RFC 3102 is an Experimental RFC from October 2001, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The companion documents are RFC 3103 and RFC 3104.

sections.title: Why RSIP
sections.content:
A NAT router must change the network layer, and possibly transport layer, header of each packet crossing it. That violates the end-to-end nature of Internet connectivity. NAT also needs an ALG for each application that embeds addresses in its payload, such as FTP.

RSIP grants a host in one addressing realm a presence in another by letting it use resources such as addresses and other routing parameters from that realm. An RSIP gateway replaces the NAT router, and RSIP-aware hosts are RSIP hosts. No ALGs are needed on the gateway for communication between an RSIP host and a host in a different realm.

The RFC says RSIP can be seen as a fix to NAT and is not a long-term solution to the IP address shortage. It does not require modifying applications, though it may not be transparent to all applications. An IESG note says costs and benefits should be weighed against other ways of relieving address shortage.
sections.eli5: A NAT is a mail clerk who rewrites every envelope. RSIP lets you borrow a proper return address so nobody has to rewrite anything.

sections.title: Architecture: Binds and Tunnels
sections.content:
A host X in address space A asks an RSIP gateway N for resources from address space B. The gateway creates a mapping called a bind between X's addressing information and the assigned resources, which lets it demultiplex inbound traffic for X. A lease time SHOULD be associated with each bind.

X tunnels its packets across space A to the gateway. The gateway is the end point of the tunnel, removes the outer header and routes the inner packet onto the public realm. For outbound packets from X to Y, the headers are an outer X -> Na followed by an inner Nb -> Y.

There are two flavors. In RSA-IP, each host leases a whole public IP address and may use any port with it. In RSAP-IP, a host leases an address, possibly shared, plus some ports. Hosts MUST NOT use addresses or ports not assigned to them.
sections.eli5: You ask the front desk for a real address, and they write it in a book. Letters go to the desk in an outer envelope, and the desk mails the inner envelope on.

sections.title: Host, Gateway and Protocol Requirements
sections.content:
An RSIP host MUST maintain virtual interfaces for leased addresses, support tunneling, and MUST NOT respond to ARPs for a public address it leases. An RSAP-IP host MUST be able to request more ports when its pool runs out. A gateway MUST support tunneling, MUST reassemble incoming fragments, and MUST time out fragments that never complete.

The gateway must route incoming packets using demultiplexing fields, such as destination IP address, IP protocol, destination TCP or UDP port, or an IPsec SPI. Encrypted fields MUST NOT be used for routing.

An RSIP protocol MUST let hosts request fields, let gateways assign them with a lease time, and let gateways reclaim them. TCP support is required in all gateways and UDP is optional. Authentication of host and gateway communication is recommended. Hosts can find a gateway by static configuration, a DHCP option or SLP.
sections.eli5: The desk has to know which of its borrowers gets each incoming letter, so every borrower gets a different label to look for, and the labels cannot be hidden in sealed envelopes.

sections.title: Deployment and Cascading
sections.content:
The RFC sketches scenarios with up to several hundred hosts behind a gateway: small or medium enterprise, residential, hospitality, dialup remote access and wireless remote access networks.

RSIP gateways can be cascaded as parent and child, and the RFC requires that RSIP MUST only assign public IP addresses. A child gateway MUST respect the constraints, such as lease time, inherited from its parent. Combining RSIP with NAT is also covered. A NAT behind or in front of RSIP means the NAT still needs ALGs and the setup cannot support IPsec. With RSIP through NAT, the NAT must not translate port numbers.
sections.eli5: Hotels, homes and offices could all use a front desk. Desks can even sit behind other desks, each passing on only what it was given.

sections.title: Interaction with Other Layer-Three Protocols
sections.content:
For IPsec, ports may be encrypted, so the 32-bit Security Parameter Index (SPI) in the AH or ESP header, which is always in the clear, is used with the assigned address to route packets. IKE hosts sharing source port 500 MUST use different initiator cookies per assigned address.

Mobile IP integration is called a topic of ongoing consideration. For Differentiated and Integrated Services, the RFC discusses tunnel handling and RSVP message translation. For multicast, the gateway MUST be multicast aware, MUST join groups on behalf of private hosts using one of its own public addresses, and MUST NOT let private addresses propagate onto the public network.
sections.eli5: Some other systems also care about addresses, such as secure tunnels, moving devices and live video. RSIP has to be taught how to play nicely with each one.

sections.title: Complications and Security
sections.content:
The RFC lists known complications. A port returned too quickly may hit a TCP TIME_WAIT state at the public host, so gateways should hold recently freed tuples for at least two minutes. Gateways must keep ICMP state. Hosts sharing an address may produce IP identification collisions when fragmenting. Two RSAP-IP hosts sharing an address cannot both run a public server on the same well-known port. Hosts also need to tell local from remote destinations, and multi-party applications have a fundamental problem for which no solution is known. Scalability is described as not well understood.

On security, RSIP does not provide security by itself. It may give the illusion of security by hiding a private address space, but security needs proper security protocols and cryptography.
sections.eli5: Borrowing addresses causes some headaches. Returned tickets can be reused too soon, two people cannot both host on the same door, and nobody has solved every party game that mixes inside and outside players.
